notes.meaning: The gatekeepers and their sons were put in charge of guarding the doors of the Lord's house by regular turns. It is called the Tent because this guarding system was first set up in King David's time, before Solomon built the stone temple. Their duty was to keep watch and protect the sacred place day and night.

The guards were stationed on all four sides: east, west, north, and south. This complete circle of posts kept the sanctuary secure from every direction. It made sure no one entered the holy area who was not supposed to be there.

Most of the gatekeepers lived in farming villages outside Jerusalem and came into town for their shifts. Each group came to serve at the house of God for seven days at a time. Every Sabbath, a new shift arrived to take over the work.

Four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, held full-time authority over the other guards. They lived right at the sanctuary and did not rotate back to the villages. They were trusted to watch over the side rooms and the temple storehouses where precious gifts and tools were kept.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Haydock explains that the four chief gatekeepers held their positions for life, rather than rotating every week like the other Levites.

notes.meaning: These chief guards slept right around the house of God so they could keep watch through the night. It was their special job to hold the keys and unlock the doors every morning. Being on site allowed them to give all their attention to protecting the holy place.

Certain Levites were placed in charge of the sacred bowls and dishes used in worship. They carefully counted every vessel when it was taken out for use and counted them again when they were returned. This careful counting kept the valuable items from being lost or mishandled.

Other Levites were assigned to look after the holy furnishings and all the daily worship supplies. They guarded the fine flour, wine, olive oil, incense, and spices. These ingredients were needed each day for the grain and drink offerings.

Only the sons of the priests were allowed to mix the sacred spices and make the holy anointing oil. God's law gave this special recipe strictly to the priests, so Levites who were not priests were not permitted to make it. This kept the special oil holy and set apart.

A Levite named Mattithiah was given the trusted job of baking the flat breads in pans for the grain offerings. He came from the family of Shallum and was personally responsible for this work. This duty ensured that the offerings were always prepared in the right way.

Another group from the Kohathite clan was responsible for the showbread. This bread consisted of twelve loaves set in rows on a golden table before the Lord. They baked fresh loaves and laid them out every Sabbath day.

The Levite musicians who led the praise lived in the temple rooms and were freed from all other duties. Their only assignment was to lead and practice sacred music continually, both day and night. This constant praise showed honor to God, who never stops doing good to His people.

These men were the heads and leaders of the Levite families according to their family trees, and they lived in Jerusalem. They stayed in the city so they could regularly direct the sacred work at God's house. Their faithful service helped the community keep worship in good order.

Jeiel was a clan leader who lived in the town of Gibeon, and his wife's name was Maacah. This verse begins a family record for King Saul, repeating a list from chapter 8. It serves as an introduction to the next chapter, which tells how Saul died.

Jeiel had ten sons, starting with his firstborn Abdon, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth. This list shows the main branches of this important family from the tribe of Benjamin. Remembering their names showed that their family line was still valued after the exile.

Mikloth was the father of Shimeam, and this branch of the family lived near their relatives in Jerusalem. Even though their ancestral hometown was Gibeon, some moved into the capital city. Living there placed them near the center of the nation's worship and community life.

Ner was the grandfather of King Saul, and Kish was Saul's father. Saul's sons included Jonathan, who was King David's loyal friend, as well as Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal. This family ruled Israel before David became king.

Jonathan had a son named Merib-baal, who is called Mephibosheth in the books of Samuel. Merib-baal became the father of Micah. Even though Saul's kingdom fell, God showed kindness to Jonathan's line and kept his descendants alive.
Micah's sons were Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. These names show how Jonathan's descendants grew into another generation. God protected this family line through many changes in Israel's history.

These verses trace Jonathan's family line down through Ahaz, Jarah, Zimri, Moza, Binea, Rephaiah, and Elasah, until it reaches Azel. Generation after generation was preserved across hundreds of years. This demonstrates that God did not forget the house of Saul, even after their kingship ended.

Azel had six sons: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. Listing all six sons brings the family tree of King Saul to a close. This record leads directly into the next chapter, which recounts the tragic end of Saul's reign and opens the way for King David.
